obligations.question: Define one concrete three-or-more-phase Bombay actor protocol and justify its relevance.
obligations.decision: Resource Pool: Initializing -> Serving -> Draining, with direction-sensitive messages (Configure IN from supervisor, Acquire/Release IN from clients, PoolReady/Granted OUT). Actor-relevant because it exercises creation (birth capability) in Initializing, peer watching in Serving, and supervised drain coordination — all actor-specific concerns beyond generic channel protocols. Distinct from the previous campaign's Worker Lifecycle.

obligations.question: List the exact invalid programs that must fail to compile and why runtime rejection is insufficient.
obligations.decision: Four invalid programs: (1) Acquire event for Initializing-phase behavior, (2) Configure event for Serving-phase behavior, (3) Acquire event for Draining-phase behavior, (4) PoolReady (outbound send) where an inbound event is expected. Runtime rejection (FSM deferral) is insufficient because deferral replays messages after phase change rather than rejecting them — a stale Configure replayed after the pool has started would reconfigure a live pool.

obligations.question: Separate actor-model laws, session-type results, Bombay derivations, policies, and application choices using primary sources.
obligations.decision: LAW: per-actor serialization (Agha 1986 §3.1.1), acquaintance addressing (Agha 1986 §3.2.1), become (Agha 1986 §3.1.3). SESSION-TYPE (not actor-model law): Honda-style duality requires both endpoints known at compile time (Honda CONCUR'93, ESOP'98) — incompatible with dynamic acquaintance. BOMBAY-DERIVED: Fsm from receive+become, Behavior::Event as single associated type. BOMBAY-POLICY: compile-time phase safety not a design goal of current algebra; Ph tracks values not types.

obligations.question: Test the concrete case against current Fsm and state precisely what it can and cannot guarantee.
obligations.decision: FSM CAN: correctly sequence phases at runtime (Initializing->Serving->Draining->Stop), defer invalid-phase messages for later replay, drain deferred messages on phase change, never drop or duplicate messages (proven by existing proptest suites). FSM CANNOT: prevent construction of invalid-phase events at compile time, distinguish inbound from outbound messages at the type level, carry Create actions (Birth=NoBirths), send typed outputs (Sends=Never).

obligations.question: Attempt a public-API derivation using Behavior, associated types, sums, products, typestate, and uninhabited types.
obligations.decision: Attempted phase-indexed typestate: _PoolBehavior<InitPhase> with Event=InitEvent, _PoolBehavior<ServingPhase> with Event=ServingEvent. Four obstructions: (1) Behavior::Event is a single associated type — each phase is a different concrete type. (2) Driver holds &mut B for single B. (3) Step::Goto(Ph) is a value, uninhabited markers have no values. (4) step() returns BehaviorActed<Self> where Self is fixed — cannot return a different phase type. Also attempted phase token gating (tokens forgeable) and PhaseProtocol trait bridging (requires flat enum). No reusable public-API derivation succeeded.

obligations.question: Record exact compiler/type/composition obstruction for every failed derivation.
obligations.decision: Five obstructions: (1) Fixed Event type — Behavior::Event is a single associated type, cannot vary by phase. (2) No runtime type change — driver holds &mut B for single B; phase transition would change B's concrete type. (3) Ph is value index not type index — Step::Goto(Ph) carries runtime value, does not constrain Event. (4) Actor addressing precludes session duality — dynamic acquaintance vs static duality. (5) Wrapper composition — every wrapper depends on single Event type; phase-varying Event would break all wrappers. Additionally: phase tokens are forgeable in safe Rust; PhaseProtocol cannot bridge to Behavior without flat enum.

obligations.question: Check Actions preservation and relevant wrapper orders, initialization, errors, termination, and births.
obligations.decision: FSM composes with Watching (confirmed by test). Fsm implements Behavior with Event=User<A,M>, Ph=Never, Birth=NoBirths, Sends=Vec<Delivery<A,Never>>. All wrappers (Watching, Supervising, At, ReceiveTimeout, Stashing, Shutdown) compose over this signature unconditionally. A phase-varying Event would require each wrapper to be generic over the phase type AND propagate phase transitions — breaking universal composition.

obligations.question: Actively try to falsify the preferred outcome with a competing derivation and adversarial examples.
obligations.decision: Competing derivation 1: Phase token gating — tokens are forgeable ZSTs; making them uninhabited prevents construction. Competing derivation 2: PhaseProtocol trait bridging — requires flat enum and runtime dispatch. Competing derivation 3: Session-type duality — fundamentally incompatible with actor acquaintance addressing (dynamic discovery vs static duality). Adversarial example: PoolMsg::Acquire sent to Initializing-phase FSM compiles, runs, is deferred — type system did not prevent it. All falsification attempts confirm the obstruction is principled.

obligations.question: Choose exactly one allowed outcome and explain why the other outcomes were rejected.
obligations.decision: Outcome: application-local. The existing FSM handles runtime phase sequencing correctly. Applications CAN build per-phase event types but cannot bridge them to the Behavior trait's single Event type while preserving both phase safety AND wrapper composition. Rejected existing-algebra-sufficient because the gap is real: per-phase types are possible but cannot integrate. Rejected minimal-core-gap because no concrete derivation failure proved an algebraic gap requiring a new primitive — the obstruction is in the Behavior trait contract, not a missing construct. New primitives would require redesigning the trait, not adding a wrapper. Rejected insufficient-evidence because the evidence is concrete: 8 tests pass, 6 derivation attempts documented, 5 obstructions enumerated with exact trait signatures.
